titleStmt.title: Buffer-Aware Analysis for Worst-Case Traversal Time of Real-Time Traffic over RRA-based NoCs

analytic.title: Buffer-Aware Analysis for Worst-Case Traversal Time of Real-Time Traffic over RRA-based NoCs

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Network-on-Chip (NoC) is a communication subsystem which has been widely utilized in many-core processors and system-on-chips in general. In order to execute time-critical applications on a NoC-based platform, the timing behavior of the network needs to be predicted during system design. One of the most important timing requirements is regarding schedulability, which refers to determining if a real-time packet can be delivered within a specific time duration. To verify the fulfillment of such timing requirement, a proper timing analysis is mandatory. Our work focuses on a Round-Robin Arbitration (RRA) based wormhole-switched NoC, which is a common architecture used in many of the existing implementations. Recursive Calculus (RC) is one of the existing analysis approaches for RRA-based NoCs which has been utilized in many research works. However, RC does not take buffer-effects into account. As a result, while performing RC on most of the existing RRA-based NoC designs, it can produce unsafe estimates which is not acceptable for time-critical systems. In this paper, we identify the optimistic problem of RC, and we propose a Revised Recursive Calculus (RRC) which extends RC by considering buffer-effects as well as supporting packetization.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Many-core architectures have been gaining growing attention nowadays due to the high computing capability along with limited hardware volume. Network-on-Chip (NoC) is a communication subsystem utilized in many-core processors and system-on-chips in general. NoC achieves communication between computing cores and other on-chip components such as I/O and memory. In order to achieve high throughput as well as low hardware cost, the wormhole-switching technique is favored for most NoC implementations [21]. Under such a technique, each packet is divided into a number of transmission units (named flits). A router can transmit a received flit without waiting for the arrival of the complete packet. Therefore, this technique incurs much lower buffer cost compared to a store-and-forward mechanism (e.g. Ethernet), which suits the design principles of on-chip networks. A number of NoC designs with different arbitration mechanisms have been proposed in the literature such as AEthereal NoC [10], timetriggered NoCs [23] [28], and fixed-priority based NoCs [29]. In this paper, we focus on Round-Robin Arbitration (RRA) based wormhole-switched NoCs, which is a common design for many existing Commercial-Off-The-Shelf (COTS) NoC implementations (e.g. Tilera TILE64 [30], Kalray MPPA R 256 [6], Adapteva Epiphany E64G401 [2]).

NoC-based many-core architectures are considered as a promising solution for future real-time systems [20]. For a real-time application, the performance does not only rely on the correctness of functionalities, but it depends on the timeliness as well. Such type of applications are thus considered to be time-critical. Many of the existing embedded systems have real-time constraints, such as a brake-by-wire system in a vehicle and a control system on an aircraft. Violation of timing requirements in such systems may result in serious consequences. Therefore, during the design phase of real-time systems, designers have to verify if all the timing requirements can be fulfilled before approving the design.

In order to execute real-time applications on a NoC-based many-core platform, the timeliness of communication over NoCs is of importance. One of the typical timing requirements of real-time applications is regarding schedulability which refers to if a real-time packet can be delivered within a specific time duration (called deadline). Targeting this type of requirement, timing analysis is typically utilized to predict the Worst-Case Traversal Time (WCTT) of each real-time packet. A number of timing analysis approaches have been proposed in the literature (e.g. [8] [9][25] [27]). Recursive Calculus (RC) [7] is one of the existing analysis methods which has been utilized in many research works (e.g. [1][3] [5][9] [19]). However, we realize a limitation of RC that it only produces safe estimates when the buffer in a NoC can hold no more than one flit. Unfortunately, such a condition is not valid for most of the existing NoC designs (e.g. TILE64 uses a buffer size of 3 flits [30], Intel SCC uses a buffer size of 24 flits [4] and MPPA R 256 uses a buffer size of 401 flits [24]). Applying RC on such type of NoCs can result in unsafe estimates (also called optimistic results hereinafter, meaning that the actual WCTT is larger than the predictions), which makes the analysis results worthless for use in hard real-time applications. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a revised RC which solves the optimistic problem of the original RC. Moreover, packetization is a mechanism commonly used in many COTS NoCs to handle large packets. However, this mechanism has not been considered in RC and its extensions. Thus, we further extend the analysis to support packetization of large packets.

div.head: A. Contribution
div.p: This paper presents the following contributions.
• A counter example is given to illustrate the optimistic problem of the original RC.
• A revised RC is proposed which resolves the identified optimistic issue.
• A further extension of RC is presented to support packetization of large packets.

div.head: B. Related Work
div.p: A number of performance analysis approaches for NoCs have been proposed in the literature aiming to guide system design and to optimize system performance, such as machine learning based methods (e.g. [26]), and queueing theory based approaches (e.g. [15][16]). However, these solutions mostly target the analysis of average latency. Consequently, they cannot be applied on applications with hard real-time requirements where the temporal behavior in the worst-case scenario is of the most importance.

Targeting hard real-time applications, the authors in [29] have presented a response time analysis for NoC messages which is based on the well-known timing analysis [13] for task scheduling on single-core processors. The authors in [14] recently proposed a stage-level latency analysis, which can provide more accurate estimates compared to the analysis presented in [29]. However, all these analyses target NoCs using a fixed-priority based arbitration, which requires implementation of sufficient virtual-channels as well as logic for priority-based scheduling. Unfortunately, to the best of our knowledge, most COTS many-core processors do not support such a design.

On the other hand, most of the existing COTS manycore processors simply use a round-robin based arbitration (e.g. Tilera TILE64 [30], Adapteva Epiphany E64G401 [2]). Targeting such type of design, several Network Calculus (NC) [17] based analyses methods have been proposed (e.g. [25][8]). However, due to the fact that a packet may span over a number of routers at the same time in a wormhole-switched NoC, using NC based approaches becomes complicated and involves significant pessimism for certain cases [9]. The authors in [27] presented an analysis approach based on Compositional Performance Analysis (CPA) [11] targeting NoCs with 2-stage iSLIP arbitration which can be used to achieve a similar analysis purpose. However, this approach does not consider the back-pressure effect (see Section III). Consequently, if back-pressure exists (e.g. in Tilera TILE64), the CPA based approach may produce optimistic results.

In [7], the authors present the RC method to compute endto-end delay of a packet over wormhole-switched networks. This work is later improved by the authors in [5], where the minimum inter-arrival times between packets are taken into account. The improved analysis thus provides much tighter estimates. In [1], the authors present another extension of RC, which considers a pipeline-effect of wormhole-switched NoCs in order to compute tighter estimates. Unfortunately, the above analyses and other works which are based on RC suffer from an optimistic problem that when each buffer in a NoC can hold more than one flit, the analysis may produce unsafe estimates. Consequently, the applicability of those works are limited in practice.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we introduce the system model considered in this paper. We recapitulate the original RC in Section III. In Section IV, we use a counter example to show the optimistic problem of RC. Section V presents the details of the revised RC. In Section VI, we use a case study to evaluate the proposed analysis, and Section VII concludes the paper along with some ideas about future work.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: The system considered in this paper consists of m × m computing cores which are connected by a wormhole-switched NoC. Figure 1 shows an abstraction of the architecture. The network uses a 2D mesh-based topology and the XY-routing mechanism, which have been widely utilized in many research works (e.g. [12][29] [22]) as well as commercial implementations (e.g. [2][30]). The access to an output link at each router is controlled by a round-robin arbitration. Under the RRA mechanism, at most one packet from each buffer can be delivered to the output-link within one round-robin cycle, thus this mechanism provides relatively fair treatment to all the packets. Each pair of adjacent routers are connected by a full-duplex link. We use bw to represent the bandwidth of each physical link and σ to denote the size of a single flit 1 . d f represents the transmission time of a single flit over one physical link (i.e. d f = σ/bw).

NoCs in the existing COTS many-core processors typically have two types of buffer architectures, being input-buffers and output-buffers. Fig. 2-a shows the router architecture of Tilera TILE64 which uses input-buffers. Each input-buffer is connected to an input-port. When a packet arrives at the input-port, it will be inserted in the corresponding inputbuffer. The router polls all the input-buffers based on a roundrobin policy. Fig. 2-b shows the router architecture of Kalray MPPA R 256 which uses output-buffers. Each output buffer is associated with an input-port and a specific output-port. When a packet arrives at a router, the router processes the routing information based on the header flit and delivers the packet to the correct output-buffer. Each output-port has an RRAbased arbiter which polls the output-buffers connected to this output-port. Different buffer architecture can result in different contention relations of traffic flows [3]. However, from the analysis point of view, the above two types of architectures can be abstracted by a unified model. While analyzing a certain traffic flow f i , each router is considered to have a number of input-ports that are connected to isolated buffers and a single output-port. The reason of considering only one output-port is that under XY-routing each flow has a fixed route. In other words, a flow can only exit a router through a fixed outputport. An example of the unified model is depicted in Fig. 3.

div.p: Buffers Output-port Fig. 3-a shows the transmission of a flow f i on TILE64, and Fig. 3-b shows the transmission of f i on MPPA R 256. We can observe that under both architectures f i has to traverse through one buffer at each router along its way to the destination. As shown in Fig. 3-c, the unified model captures the transmission of f i through the route. As long as the network can be captured by this unified model, the analysis presented in this paper is always valid. To simplify the presentation, in the following sections we use Kalray MPPA R 256 as an example to illustrate the proposed analysis. The network contains a set of n periodic or sporadic real-

div.p: Each flow includes an infinite number of packets (also called instances hereinafter) with the same characteristics. L i represents the packet size of f i (including the payload and the header). T i denotes the period of a periodic flow or the minimum inter-arrival time of a sporadic flow. Each flow has a relative deadline D i . A flow is defined as schedulable if its WCTT (denoted by W i ) is no larger than its relative deadline (i.e. W i ≤ D i ). The whole flow set is defined as schedulable if all the flows can meet their deadlines. Each flow also has a fixed path/route R i which starts from its source node (denoted as Sr i ) and ends at its destination (denoted as Ds i ).

div.head: IV. OPTIMISTIC RESULTS IN RC
div.p: In this section, we present a counter example to show that the original RC can produce unsafe analysis results (i.e. the actual WCTT of a flow can be larger than the computed estimate) when the buffer can hold multiple flits.

Assume that there are four flows in the network, and f 1 is the flow under analysis. The transmission route of each flow is shown in Fig. 4. Now we consider the computation of the maximum transmission delay of f 1 over its first link (i.e. the link connected to router A through its local input-port). As discussed before, the delay of f 1 over its first link depends on its delay over the following links along its route. According to the routes of the flows, both f 2 and f 3 can block f 1 at the output-port of router A. As presented in Section III, since f 2 and f 3 enter router A from the same input-link (i.e. through the southern input-port), RC only takes the one which can cause the maximum blocking delay into account. The computation can be derived as follows.

div.p: The computation implies that either f 2 or f 3 can block f 1 at a time (i.e. f 2 and f 3 cannot block f 1 at the same time). Unfortunately, the above calculation does not cover the actual worst-case. Considering the scenario depicted in Fig. 4, when f 1 arrives at router A, f 2 is occupying Link(AB). After transmitting one flit of f 2 to router B, the buffer at router B becomes full because f 3 which is queued ahead of f 2 takes up the rest of the buffer. At the same time, the header of f 3 is blocked by f 4 at an output-port of router C. As a result, the transmission of f 4 blocks f 3 , that indirectly blocks f 2 and f 1 . In this case, both f 2 and f 3 can cause blocking to f 1 at the same time. Therefore, RC, which considers blocking from either f 2 or f 3 , produces an optimistic estimate.

div.head: V. REVISED RECURSIVE CALCULUS
div.p: In this section, we present a Revised Recursive Calculus (RRC) targeting RRA-based wormhole-switched NoCs. The proposed analysis improves the original RC from the following aspects:
• addressing the optimistic problem;
• supporting packetization of large packets.

div.head: A. Removing Optimism
div.p: First, we solve the optimistic problem that is involved in the original RC. The main reason of the incurred optimism is that buffer sizes are not considered correctly. In the example presented in Section IV, RC only works if the buffer of router B is small enough such that when the header flit of f 2 is inserted in the buffer, no flit of f 3 can stay in this buffer at the same time. In other words, flits of f 2 and f 3 cannot be in the buffer of router B at the same time. In this case, only one of these two flows can cause blocking to f 1 . However, once the buffer can hold more than one flit, that is actually the case for most of the existing NoC designs (e.g. the buffer size of Intel SCC is 24 flits [4], and each buffer in a Tilera TILE64 router can hold at most 3 flits [30]), the above condition will not be valid any more.

For the example shown in Fig. 4, in order to compute the maximum transmission delay of f 1 over Link(AB), we need to consider the case that f 1 loses in the round-robin arbitration (i.e. each of the other buffers can transmit one packet ahead of f 1 ). This consideration has been covered in the original RC. Assume that f 2 is the flow which wins the current arbitration on Link(AB). In addition to the above condition, we also need to consider that when f 2 is about to transmit flits to router B, the buffer connected to Link(AB) at router B is full. This additional consideration is missing in RC.
In summary, while computing the WCTT of f 1 (i.e. d( f 1 , l 1 1 )), we need to take the following types of delay into account:
• the delay of f 1 to traverse Link(AB) and the following links along its route R 1 ;

• the delay of the flows, that win the round-robin arbitration over f 1 at router A, to traverse Link(AB) and the following links along their routes; • the delay of the flows in the buffer at router B to traverse Link(BC) and the following links along their routes (i.e. delay cost for emptying the buffer, also called buffer delay hereinafter).

RC has already taken the first two types of delay into account (i.e. line 15 and line 11 in Alg. 2 respectively), and only the third type of delay is missing. Below we present how to add the missing buffer delay into RC.

We use ϕ to represent the size of the buffer connected to each input-port. In order to compute the delay of the flows in the buffer at router B to traverse Link(BC), we need to first find out which flows can appear in the buffer. Since each buffer is associated with a specific input-port, the flows that can appear in this buffer must come from router A. Flows can have different packet sizes, thus the buffer can contain different combinations of packets (e.g. a buffer may contain 2 packets from f 2 and 1 packet from f 3 , or 1 packet from f 2 and 2 packets from f 3 at the same time). As we know, different flows can also have different traversal delays over Link(BC) due to their distinctive routes. Therefore, different combinations of packets in a buffer can result in different delay to empty the buffer. In this paper, we propose two approaches to compute the delay caused by the above buffer effect.

The first approach is to use Integer Linear Programming (ILP) to find the maximum buffer delay. ILP is a tool to solve an optimization problem of an objective with certain constraints. In the context of analyzing the buffer delay, we can consider finding the maximum buffer delay as the objective of the ILP. Before defining the expression of the maximum buffer delay for a certain buffer, we first present a theorem regarding the buffer state in the worst-case.

div.head: Theorem 1. A buffer with a given size of ϕ can hold no more than two partial packets. When a buffer holds only one partial packet which is at the head of the buffer, the corresponding buffer delay results in the maximum traversal delay of the packet under analysis.
div.p: Proof. The first statement can be proven by contradiction. If the packets queued in the buffer excluding the one at the head and the one at the end are partial packets, the transmission of these packets must be preempted by other packets. This contradicts to the fact that the considered NoCs use a nonpreemptive transmission policy. Therefore, there can be at most two partial packets exist in the buffer, and they can only be the one at the head and the one at the end. Based on the number of partial packets in the buffer, there are four possible cases: Case 1: there is no partial packets Case 2: there is one partial packet which is at the head of the buffer Case 3: there is one partial packet which is at the end of the buffer Case 4: there are two partial packets First, we need to clarify that for a packet which is partially queued in the buffer, we still use its complete packet size to compute its traversal delay over the following links in order to simplify the calculation. We now prove that Case 2 (as shown in Fig. 5) always gives the maximum traversal delay to the packet under analysis. For Case 1: If we move the packet at the head forward (i.e. a part of this packet has been transmitted to the next hop, becoming Case 2), a free space in the buffer will increase. Based on the clarification presented earlier, as long as we keep a part of this packet in the buffer, the delay caused by this packet to the packet under analysis remain the same. No matter if the extra free space can allow the buffer to hold more packets or not, the buffer delay does not decrease. Therefore, Case 1 cannot produce a larger buffer delay compared to Case 2. For Case 3: Since a part of the packet at the end is in the buffer, the rest of this packet must be in the buffer at the previous hop. As a result, in the current round-robin cycle for l x (where l x is the input-link of the buffer under analysis), no other packet from the same input-buffer at the previous hop can use l x . If we move this packet forward such that it is completely in the buffer under analysis (i.e. it becomes the same as Case 1), another packet from the same input-buffer can be transmitted on l x ahead of the packet under analysis in the current round-robin cycle. Therefore, Case 3 gives smaller buffer delay compared to Case 1. Based on the proof of Case 1, Case 3 cannot produce larger buffer delay than Case 2 either. For Case 4: This case can be proven in the same manner as Case 3.

div.p: Based on the above discussion, we can conclude that when a buffer holds only one partial packet which is at the head of the buffer, the corresponding buffer delay gives the maximum traversal delay of the packet under analysis. Now we derive the expression for the maximum buffer delay for a certain buffer. According to Theorem 1, the maximum buffer delay occurs when the buffer holds only one partial packet which is at the head of the buffer. As stated earlier, for a packet which is partially queued in the buffer, we still use its complete packet size to compute its traversal delay over the following links. Given a fixed buffer size, decreasing the number of flits of the first packet queued in the buffer can increase the space in the buffer to hold more complete packets, which can result in larger buffer delay. Therefore, to maximize the buffer delay, we need to minimize the number of flits of the first packet in the buffer, which is one flit. Definition 1. The approximation-based approach can result in more pessimistic estimates, but it produces results faster than using ILP especially for large systems. During the design phase of a system, we can first use the approximation-based approach to perform a fast analysis of given NoC traffic. If the results already show that all the flows can meet their deadlines, we can directly approve the current design. On the other hand, if the analysis gives negative results, we can then perform the ILP-based analysis to calculate more accurate estimates.

Using the ILP-based approach or Eq. 2, we can obtain an upper-bound of the delay to empty a certain buffer. We then add this delay into RC. As discussed in Section III, the intuition of RC is to recursively compute the traversal delay of a flow link by link. The buffer effect presented above can happen on any router in the network. div.head: B. Supporting Packetization
div.p: In order to achieve a more reliable transmission and a fair distribution of bandwidth, most of the existing NoCs apply a packetization mechanism on large packets. In other words, these NoCs divide a large packet into a number of smaller subpackets during the transmission. For example, the maximum packet size over Tilera TILE64 is between a few flits and 128 flits [30]; for Kalray MPPA R 256, the packet size is up to 62 flits on the Data-NoC and 2 flits on the Control-NoC. For this type of NoCs, RC which considers each packet as one non-preemptive segment cannot be utilized directly because it can produce incorrect results. For example, in RC, when a packet is at the head of a buffer on a certain router, it only needs to wait for one round-robin cycle until it gets access to the output-port. However, if this packet is divided into m subpackets during its transmission, it actually needs to wait for up to m round-robin cycles until the last sub-packet gets access to the output-link. Therefore, in order to make the analysis more practical targeting COTS NoCs, we revise RC to support NoCs with packetization. The revised analysis (named RRC), is illustrated in Alg. 3&4.

Under the packetization mechanism, the finishing time of the transmission of each packet is the time when the last sub-packet completely arrives at its destination. Based on the original packet size of f i (i.e. L i ) and the size of each subpacket after packetization (i.e. θ), we can compute the number of sub-packets with size of θ (Alg. 3, line 4). Note that, if L i -1 is not an integer multiple of θ -1, the size of the last sub-packet (denoted as L last i ) will be smaller than θ (Alg. 3, line 5). Since the transmissions of sub-packets through the NoC are independent from each other, we can consider that the last sub-packet of f i is the packet under analysis, and the rest of sub-packets are regular packets generated from the same source node and released ahead (Alg. 3, line 7-11).

div.head: VI. EVALUATION
div.p: We have performed a case study to evaluate the proposed analysis-RRC. The case study is based on an autonomous vehicle application. The considered sub-system contains a number of tasks performing different functionalities including obstacle detection, navigation control, stability control and so on. There are 14 real-time flows used for inter-task communication. The sub-system is deployed on a 3 × 3 2D-mesh based NoC platform. Each buffer has a depth of 3 flits, and the size of each sub-packet is limited to 128 flits (i.e. similar to the setting of Tilera TILE64). The mapping of tasks and the flow information are presented in Fig. 6. A cycle-based simulator which simulates packet transmission over RRA-based NoCs is implemented using Python. We compare the analysis results produced by RC and RRC with the observations from simulations. For each flow, the observation is based on 1300 collected samples.

( The results are depicted in Fig. 7 and Table I. First, we can observe that for f 2 and f 11 , the estimates computed by RC are smaller than the simulation observations. This clearly shows the optimistic problem of the original RC that has been discussed in Section IV. On the other hand, RRC always provides safe estimates, even though it is pessimistic for certain flows. When a flow does not suffer from the buffer effect (e.g. f 6 , f 10 , and f 14 ), RC and RRC give the same analysis results. Moreover, we also notice that the ILP-based and the approximation-based approaches produce the same estimates in this case study. This is because the buffer size is small such that each buffer can hold no more than 2 packets from the given flows. Considering the fact that most of the COTS NoCs tend to use small buffers due to the limitation of hardware volume, the approximation-based approach can achieve similar applicability as the ILP-based method.

Even though RRC gives safe analysis results, we can observe that RRC indeed incurs pessimism in the computed estimates. The main source of pessimism is that inter-arrival times between successive packets of each flow are not considered in the analysis. In [5], the authors have presented an extension of RC called Branch, Prune and Collapse (BPC) algorithm where the periodic arrival pattern of packets is taken into account. The technique proposed in [5] can be applied on RRC as well to produce tighter analysis results. However, this is out of the scope of this paper.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORKS
div.p: In this paper, we identify the optimistic problem involved in the Recursive Calculus which is an analysis approach used to compute the worst-case traversal delay of traffic over RRA-based NoCs. We propose a Revised Recursive Calculus which extends RC by taking buffer-effects into account and supporting packetization of large packets. A case study based on an autonomous vehicle application is performed to evaluate the proposed analysis. The case study clearly shows the unsafe estimates produced by RC. On the other hand, the estimates computed by RRC are always higher than the observations from simulation.

Even though RRC provides guaranteed analysis results, it indeed includes pessimism which can lead to overdimensioning at the resources. In the future work, we need to further improve RRC by reducing the involved pessimism. Potential solutions are to use the techniques presented in [5] [18] to take into account arrival patterns of traffic.
